According to one survey by the Government of Canada, 30 per cent of respondents had experienced sexual harassment in the workplace in the past two years.

How Common is Sexual Harassment?
*   77 per cent of women had experienced verbal sexual harassment.
*   51 per cent of women had been sexually touched without permission.
*   41 per cent said they had been sexually harassed online.
*   27 per cent said they had survived sexual assault.
Anita Hill, an academic and attorney, stated that "45 per cent of employees in the private workforce say they experience sexual harassment" and that the majority of victims are women.
The Canadian Labour Congress reported that nearly seven in 10 workers have experienced a form of harassment and violence in the workplace.
Nearly one in two had experienced sexual harassment and violence in the past two years.
When looking at data from individual countries from 2019, 68 percent of women surveyed in Germany reported having been exposed to sexual harassment in the workplace over the course of their lifetime.
The lifetime number was similar in Spain (66 per cent), however, when asked who had been exposed to sexual harassment in the workplace in the past 12 months, 31 per cent indicated they had.

A separate study in Europe found that 72 per cent of women were the victims of sexual harassment by someone they didn't know, with most incidents happening when out in public.

In one 2018 survey that looked at the public transport system in New York City, researchers found 75 per cent of female respondents reported experiencing harassment (including sexual) and theft while using public transportation.
In the UK, sexual harassment on the London Underground increased 42 per cent between 2015 and 2019.
In a 2022 survey focused on harassment that occurred on the Toronto Transit System, it was found that 86 per cent of riders had experienced some form of harassment.
Women (59 per cent) were more than twice as likely as men (22 per cent) to experience unwanted sexual looks or gestures.

In the two years following the the prominent #MeToo social media movement, EEOC saw a significant increase in sexual harassment reports, due to people being inspired to speak out about their experiences of sexual harassment.

#### Do you know the definitions and signs of different harassment types?
When examining sexual harassment statistics, one thing that becomes apparent is that often there is disparity in how women and men perceive sexual harassment.
A survey conducted by The Barna Group found major differences in the ways that men and women view sexual harassment.
When presented with a list of 20 behaviors (ranging from groping to whistling), in all but one case **men were less likely than women to label an act as sexual harassment**.
The one exception was a tie: 12 per cent of men and women labeled light-hearted flirting as sexual harassment.
A good illustration of this point is how someone pushing against you on public transit was seen as sexual harassment by 70 per cent of women, however, only 52 per cent of men thought so.
The genders also disagreed on sexual comments about a person's looks or body.
Here, 86 per cent of women said it was sexual harassment, versus 70 per cent of men.
This is the case worldwide.
The Ottawa Citizen reported that 83 per cent of male survey respondents said being asked out repeatedly by a coworker (after they already said no) is sexual harassment.
Interestingly, fewer females agreed with that notion (78 per cent).
In that same survey, 27 per cent of women said making comments about clothing or appearance is sexual harassment. 18 per cent of men agreed.
What are the Trends?
Emily Martin of the National Women's Law Center states that women experience harassment more when they work in industries where they're seen as "out of place" (like construction).
Low- paying jobs (like a nanny) and service-based industries (like fast food) also see higher than average levels of harassment.
Safer America compiled various sexual harassment statistics to highlight which industries see the highest occurrences of sexual harassment.
*   **Restaurants and hospitality** make up roughly 25 per cent of all sexual harassment reports filed to EEOC.
*   **Nursing** accounts for nearly 12 per cent of EEOC sexual harassment reports.
*   While 60 per cent of nurses have reported experiencing some form of sexual harassment, only 27 per cent decided to report it to their employer.
*   58 per cent of people in **academia** (students, staff and faculty) reported having been sexually harassed.
*   Women aged 18 to 24 enrolled in college are three times more likely than any other group of women to be sexual assault victims.
*   Medical students also reported that 36 per cent of them had experienced sexual harassment from faculty and staff.
Of the different industries where sexual harassment is more common, the military continues to see one of the biggest disparities between the genders when looking at sexual harassment statistics.
*   Among active duty women, 23 per cent experience sexual harassment, versus four per cent of men.
*   Among veterans, 41 per cent of women reported sexual harassment or assault, while four per cent men have.
Why Are Victims Staying Silent?
The true cost of sexual harassment isn't fully accounted for when looking at sexual harassment statistics.

While numbers like loss of wages or benefits can be forecasted, there are other costs that can never be fully calculated, like the loss of earning potential from having your career derailed due to sexual harassment.

In 2021, the TIME'S UP Foundation and the Institute for Women's Policy Research partnered together on a new report, "Paying Today and Tomorrow: Charting the Financial Costs of Workplace Sexual Harassment." A key finding from the report was that sexual harassment in the workplace can cost an individual anywhere **from a few hundred dollars to $1.3 million** over a lifetime.
Between 2018 and 2021, EEEO recovered an estimated 300 million dollars for individuals with sexual harassment claims through resolved charge receipts and in litigation.

While it is hopeful to see some victims get financial compensation for their sexual harassment claims, these numbers only reflect the small percentage of sexual harassment that is actually reported and complaints that are pursued.
A company's culture sets the tone for acceptable behavior.
When that culture tolerates or overlooks misconduct, harassment can quickly take root and spread.
Even without explicit encouragement, subtle signals from leadership, policies, or day-to-day practices can create an environment where harassment is enabled.
When offensive comments, exclusionary practices, or demeaning jokes are brushed off as "harmless" or "just part of the culture," it sends a clear message: disrespect is acceptable.

Over time, this normalizes inappropriate behavior and discourages individuals from speaking up. **Action Tip:** Establish and enforce clear behavioral standards that apply equally to everyone, regardless of rank or tenure.
If those who engage in harassment are rarely disciplined-or worse, rewarded with promotions-others may believe that bad behavior has no real consequences.

A lack of visible accountability erodes trust and deters victims from reporting incidents. **Action Tip:** Respond consistently and transparently to misconduct, ensuring that accountability is non-negotiable across all levels of the organization.
Cultures with rigid hierarchies or unchecked power dynamics can foster environments where harassment goes unchallenged.

Employees may fear retaliation, career damage, or social isolation if they report concerns about higher-ups. **Action Tip:** Empower employees with safe, confidential reporting channels and reinforce anti-retaliation policies in both training and practice.
If employees are unclear about what constitutes harassment-or how to report it-misconduct can thrive unchecked.

Limited training, inconsistent messaging, and unclear policies leave employees vulnerable and ill-equipped to act. **Action Tip:** Offer regular, engaging training sessions that go beyond legal definitions to include real-world scenarios and practical guidance.
An organization that values loyalty and image over transparency may actively discourage individuals from coming forward.

Whistleblowers might be labeled as "troublemakers," and concerns swept under the rug to "protect" the brand. **Action Tip:** Foster a speak-up culture by celebrating ethical courage and responding to concerns with seriousness and respect, not defensiveness.

What percentage of people have been sexually harassed?

Sexual harassment affects a significant portion of the population, with various surveys and studies indicating that a substantial number of individuals, particularly women, have experienced sexual harassment in different settings.
What percent of females are sexually harassed?

According to sexual harassment statistics compiled from multiple sources, a considerable percentage of females, ranging from 54% to 81%, have reported experiencing sexual harassment, with incidents including verbal harassment, unwanted touching, and online harassment.
Who is more likely to be sexually harassed?
Women, especially those working in industries where they are perceived as "out of place," low-paying jobs, and service-based sectors, are more likely to experience sexual harassment.
Additionally, individuals in male-dominated industries and those who rely on tips as their primary source of income are disproportionately affected by sexual harassment.
What happens when someone faces sexual harassment?
When someone goes through sexual harassment, it can really affect them-mentally, emotionally, and even financially.
Many people feel stressed, anxious, or scared to go to work.
Some might even leave their job to avoid the person harassing them.
In some cases, their career progress can take a hit, especially if they're not supported or taken seriously.
It's also common for people to stay quiet about what happened out of fear-fear of being judged, losing their job, or not being believed.
That's why it's so important for workplaces to have safe and clear ways to report harassment and offer support right away.
Why do companies need sexual harassment training?
Sexual harassment training helps everyone understand what's okay and what's not in the workplace.
It's not just about rules-it's about building a respectful and safe environment where people feel comfortable and valued.
Training shows employees how to recognize harassment, how to report it, and what to do if they see it happening.
For managers, it teaches them how to respond the right way and protect their team.
Without training, people might not even realize certain behaviors are harmful-or they might not know what steps to take if something happens.
Can companies be sued for ignoring harassment?
Yes, they absolutely can.
If someone reports harassment and the company doesn't take it seriously or fails to act, they can face legal consequences.
In some cases, that means paying large fines or being taken to court.
But beyond the legal risks, ignoring harassment damages a company's reputation and trust with employees.
By addressing harassment properly-and early-companies show they care about their people, and that makes all the difference in building a healthy workplace.
Why don't people report sexual harassment?
Many people don't report sexual harassment because they're scared.
They worry they might lose their job, be treated badly, or not be believed.
Some people think speaking up won't change anything or that the company will protect the person who caused the problem.
Others feel ashamed or want to just move on and forget it happened.
Sometimes, the company doesn't have a clear way to report issues, which makes it even harder.
That's why it's so important for employers to create a safe and supportive reporting process.
What percentage of workers report sexual harassment?
Only about 1 in 3 workers who experience sexual harassment actually report it.
That means most people stay quiet, even if something serious happened.
In some surveys, the number is even lower-closer to 1 in 4.
The main reasons people don't report include fear of retaliation, not trusting HR or management, and not wanting to be seen as a troublemaker.
